details: Science begins with curiosity about everyday surroundings—such as why fruits taste sour, why turmeric turns red with soap, why ice melts, or how plants grow. Scientific investigation follows a structured cycle: observing natural phenomena, formulating hypotheses, conducting hands-on activities, making careful measurements, and drawing evidence-based conclusions. Scientific discoveries often spark new questions, driving an ever-evolving body of knowledge.
evidence_or_examples: Physics, chemistry, biology, and earth science are deeply interlinked. For example, the physical process of heat flow directly drives atmospheric water cycles in earth science and transpiration in biological systems.

sub_branches.concept: To foster scientific questioning and inquiry by investigating everyday natural phenomena.
details: Observe an everyday natural event in your home or school environment.
Formulate three specific 'Why' or 'How' questions regarding the observed event.
Propose a simple, safe experimental test to investigate one of your questions.
Observation: Systematic observation and questioning reveal underlying cause-and-effect relationships in daily phenomena.
evidence_or_examples: Scientific knowledge develops through structured questioning, hypothesis testing, and continuous evidence evaluation.

details: Scientific Inquiry: A systematic approach to understanding the natural world through observation, hypothesis formulation, experimentation, and evidence analysis.
evidence_or_examples: Testing why ice melts faster on metal than on plastic.

chapters.chapter_title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

mind_map.root_topic: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

details: Substances around us are categorized by their nature: Group A (Acidic: lemon juice, vinegar, tamarind, amla), Group B (Basic: soap solution, baking soda, lime water), and Group C (Neutral: distilled water, sugar solution, common salt solution). Testing must be done using indicators rather than tasting unknown chemicals for safety.
evidence_or_examples: Turmeric belongs to the ginger family (Curcuma longa). Apart from culinary use, its active pigment curcumin acts as a natural pH indicator.

details: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens. Blue litmus paper turns red in acidic media. Red litmus paper turns blue in basic media. Turmeric paper turns red in basic media but remains yellow in acidic and neutral media. Red rose extract turns magenta/red in acids and green in bases.
evidence_or_examples: Write a message using lemon juice on white paper. Spraying red rose extract or red cabbage juice over the paper reveals the secret message in bright red/pink.

sub_branches.concept: To classify household liquid samples as acidic, basic, or neutral using litmus indicators.
details: Place a drop of each liquid sample on separate strips of blue and red litmus paper using a clean dropper.
Observe and record any immediate or gradual color changes.
Categorize samples based on color response.
Observation: Lemon juice and vinegar turn blue litmus red (Acidic). Soap and baking soda turn red litmus blue (Basic). Water produces no change on either paper (Neutral).
evidence_or_examples: Litmus paper explicitly differentiates acidic (blue->red), basic (red->blue), and neutral (no change) media.

sub_branches.concept: To prepare and test a natural indicator solution from red rose petals.
details: Soak fresh red rose petals in warm water until the water acquires a distinct pink/red color.
Filter the solution to obtain a clear liquid indicator.
Add 5 drops of extract to test tubes containing lemon juice and baking soda solution separately.
Observation: The extract turns dark pink/magenta in lemon juice and bright green in baking soda solution.
evidence_or_examples: Red rose petal extract is an effective natural multi-color indicator for identifying acids and bases.

details: Acidic Substance: A substance with a sour taste that turns blue litmus paper red.
Basic Substance: A substance with a bitter taste, soapy feel, that turns red litmus paper blue.
Acid-Base Indicator: A substance that exhibits distinct color changes when exposed to acidic or basic solutions.
evidence_or_examples: Lemon juice, citric acid, acetic acid (vinegar).
Litmus, turmeric, phenolphthalein.

branches.theme: Section 3.1 & 3.2 Torchlight, Electric Cell, and Battery

details: A torch comprises a bulb, reflector, switch, and electric cells enclosed in a body. Electric cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy. Connecting the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of another forms a battery. Reversing terminal orientation breaks current flow.
evidence_or_examples: Global engineering bodies (IEC, ANSI, IEEE) standardized circuit schematic symbols so technical blueprints can be universally read across all countries.

branches.theme: Section 3.3 Circuit Diagrams and LED Properties

details: A circuit diagram represents components using symbols: long thin line = positive cell terminal; short thick line = negative terminal. An LED has two unequal leads; current flows only when the longer lead connects to the positive supply and shorter lead to negative supply.
evidence_or_examples: Connecting an LED in reverse polarity blocks current flow entirely, preventing light emission and potentially damaging sensitive components.

sub_branches.concept: To construct a simple functional switch using safety pins and drawing pins.
details: Insert one drawing pin through the ring end of a safety pin and press into cardboard.
Fix the second drawing pin on cardboard such that the free end of the safety pin can touch it.
Connect wires from the drawing pins to complete a circuit with a cell and bulb.
Rotate the safety pin to touch (ON) or leave a gap (OFF).
Observation: When safety pin touches second drawing pin, circuit completes and bulb glows. When rotated away, gap breaks circuit and bulb turns off.
evidence_or_examples: A switch regulates current flow by closing or opening the electrical circuit gap.

details: Electric Current Direction: Conventional current flows from the positive (+) terminal of the power source to the negative (-) terminal.
LED (Light Emitting Diode): A semiconductor light source that permits electric current flow in only one forward direction.
evidence_or_examples: Flow of charge in closed cell-bulb circuit.
Energy-efficient indicator lamps and displays.

chapters.chapter_title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

mind_map.root_topic: The World of Metals and Non-metals

details: Malleability allows materials to be hammered into thin sheets (gold, silver, aluminium). Ductility allows drawing into thin wires (copper, iron). Metallic lustre gives fresh surfaces shiny reflection. Sonority produces ringing sound on striking.
evidence_or_examples: Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a butter knife. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

branches.theme: Section 4.2 Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and Water

sub_branches.concept: 4.2 Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and Water
details: Magnesium ribbon burns in oxygen with blinding white light to yield Magnesium Oxide (MgO), which dissolves in water forming Mg(OH)2 (turns red litmus blue = Basic). Sulfur burns forming Sulfur Dioxide (SO2), forming sulfurous acid in water (turns blue litmus red = Acidic). Iron rusts in moist air forming brown hydrated iron oxide.
evidence_or_examples: Everything in the universe is constructed from 118 chemical elements cataloged in the periodic table.

sub_branches.concept: To test materials for malleability by hammering.
details: Place each sample on an anvil surface.
Strike each sample firmly 3-4 times with a hammer.
Observe whether sample flattens into a sheet or breaks into pieces.
Observation: Iron nail and copper wire flatten into thin sheets without breaking. Coal and sulfur lump shatter into fine powder.
evidence_or_examples: Metals possess malleability (flatten under impact), while solid non-metals are brittle.

details: Malleability: The property of a material allowing it to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.
Ductility: The property of a material enabling it to be drawn into thin wires.
evidence_or_examples: Aluminium foil for food packaging; gold foil.
Copper and copper alloy wires in electrical grids.

chapters.chapter_title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

mind_map.root_topic: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

details: Physical changes involve state or structural shifts where molecules remain unchanged. Chemical changes break and form chemical bonds, accompanied by energy evolution/absorption, gas emission, color shifts, or precipitation.
evidence_or_examples: Michael Faraday delivered famous lectures on 'The Chemical History of a Candle', demonstrating that candle burning involves both physical wax melting and chemical wax combustion.

sub_branches.concept: To classify vegetable prep and composting activities as physical or chemical changes.
details: Chop fresh vegetables and peel potato skins.
Collect vegetable peels in an earthen pot mixed with moist soil and leave for 3 weeks.
Observe changes in vegetable shape versus organic peel decomposition.
Observation: Chopping changes vegetable size/shape (Physical). Peel decomposition converts organic matter into dark nutrient-rich humus (Chemical).
evidence_or_examples: Mechanical operations alter physical state without new substance creation; biological decay forms chemically new substances.

details: Physical Change: A change in which a material undergoes alteration in physical form without creating any chemically new substance.
Chemical Change: A process where chemical bonds are broken and formed, yielding one or more distinct new substances.
evidence_or_examples: Freezing water into ice blocks; crushing a can.
Combustion of LPG gas; digestion of food.

chapters.chapter_title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

mind_map.root_topic: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

branches.theme: Section 6.1 & 6.2 Puberty Changes and Endocrine Control

details: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Pituitary gland acts as the master gland, stimulating thyroid, adrenals, testes (testosterone), and ovaries (estrogen). Sweat and sebaceous gland hyperactivation causes adolescent acne.
evidence_or_examples: Adolescents require iron-rich foods (leafy greens, jaggery, meat) to prevent anemia during rapid blood volume expansion and menstruation.

sub_branches.concept: To record and analyze growth velocity (height and weight changes) in adolescent boys and girls.
details: Measure height (cm) and body weight (kg) of 10 boys and 10 girls aged 11 to 15.
Calculate average height and weight for each age group.
Plot growth curves against age on graph paper.
Observation: Girls frequently show earlier growth spurts between ages 11-13 compared to boys, but boys catch up and often exceed girls in height by age 15-16.
evidence_or_examples: Adolescent growth spurts occur at varying onset times between sexes, governed by endocrine hormone surges.

details: Adolescence: The period of transition from childhood to adulthood (ages 10-19) accompanied by physical and reproductive maturation.
Hormones: Chemical messengers secreted directly into blood by ductless endocrine glands to regulate target organ functions.
evidence_or_examples: Human pubertal development stage.
Thyroxin, Insulin, Testosterone, Estrogen.

details: Conduction dominates in solids (metals conduct rapidly). Convection occurs in fluids; heated fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises while denser cool fluid sinks. Radiation transfers heat through vacuum at speed of light.
evidence_or_examples: A lightweight paper spiral suspended above a lit candle rotates continuously as rising warm air convection currents strike its blades.

details: Land has a lower specific heat capacity than water, heating and cooling much faster. Daytime: Land heats rapidly; hot air rises, pulling cool air from sea (Sea Breeze). Nighttime: Land cools rapidly; warm air over sea rises, pulling cool air from land (Land Breeze).
evidence_or_examples: Paper tightly wrapped around a copper rod does not char easily over a flame because copper quickly conducts heat away from the paper.

sub_branches.concept: To visualize fluid convection currents using a potassium permanganate (KMnO4) crystal in water.
details: Fill beaker with clean water.
Use a straw to carefully deposit a KMnO4 crystal at the bottom center of beaker.
Apply heat directly under the crystal using a small candle flame.
Observation: Purple streams of dissolved KMnO4 rise vertically from the bottom, spread horizontally at the top surface, and descend down the cooler beaker walls.
evidence_or_examples: Heating creates density-driven circular fluid convection currents.

details: Convection: Heat transfer in liquids and gases caused by physical movement of fluid due to temperature and density gradients.
Sea Breeze: A cool wind blowing from the sea toward the land during daytime.
evidence_or_examples: Boiling water in a pot; atmospheric winds.
Natural cooling of coastal cities during sunny days.

branches.theme: Section 8.1 & 8.2 Time Measurement and Simple Pendulum

details: A simple pendulum consists of a small metallic bob suspended from a rigid stand by a light string. One complete back-and-forth movement is one oscillation. Time period (T) is the time taken to complete one oscillation, determined solely by string length.
evidence_or_examples: To convert speed from km/h to m/s, multiply by (5/18). To convert from m/s to km/h, multiply by (18/5).

sub_branches.concept: To measure and verify the constancy of a simple pendulum's time period.
details: Set up pendulum suspended from clamp stand.
Displace bob 5 cm to one side from mean position and release gently.
Measure total time for 20 complete oscillations using stopwatch.
Calculate Time Period T = Total Time / 20.
Observation: Total time for 20 oscillations remains nearly identical across multiple trials (~40 seconds for 1m length, T = 2.0 s).
evidence_or_examples: The time period of a simple pendulum of fixed length is constant (isochronous periodic motion).

details: Speed Formula: Speed (v) = Distance (d) / Time (t).
Time Period (T): The time taken by a pendulum or oscillating system to complete one full back-and-forth oscillation.
evidence_or_examples: Calculating vehicle velocity.
Pendulum clock timing.

branches.theme: Section 9.1 & 9.2 Human Digestion and Cellular Respiration

details: Saliva contains amylase breaking starch to sugar. Stomach secretes HCl (kills microbes) and pepsin (digests proteins). Small intestine receives liver bile (emulsifies fats) and pancreatic juice. Microscopic villi maximize absorption area. Cellular respiration: Glucose + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + ATP energy.
evidence_or_examples: Ancient Indian medical text Charaka Samhita highlighted that health depends on 'Agni' (digestive fire) and recommended digestive spices like ginger and black pepper.

sub_branches.concept: To measure and compare human breathing rates during rest versus after intense physical exercise.
details: Count number of breaths (1 inhalation + 1 exhalation = 1 breath) per minute while sitting at rest.
Perform brisk running or jumping jacks for 5 minutes.
Count breathing rate immediately after exercise and after 5 minutes rest.
Observation: Resting breathing rate is ~15-18 breaths/min. Post-exercise breathing rate surges to ~25-30 breaths/min.
evidence_or_examples: Physical exercise increases cellular energy demand, accelerating breathing rate to supply extra oxygen for cellular respiration.

details: Cellular Respiration Equation: Glucose + Oxygen -> Carbon Dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP).
Villi: Finger-like vascularized projections lining the inner wall of the small intestine that maximize nutrient absorption surface area.
evidence_or_examples: Metabolic energy generation in cells.
Nutrient absorption into bloodstream.

details: Starch test using iodine solution turns leaves blue-black, proving photosynthetic glucose synthesis. Xylem consists of dead tracheids and vessels operating via transpiration pull. Phloem consists of living sieve tubes actively moving sucrose.
evidence_or_examples: Pioneering Indian woman biochemist who discovered cytochrome C in plant cellular respiration at Cambridge University and analyzed the high nutritional value of Neera.

sub_branches.concept: To test a green leaf for the presence of starch produced via photosynthesis.
details: Boil leaf in water for 3 minutes to break cell membranes.
Place leaf in a tube with ethanol and heat in a boiling water bath until chlorophyll dissolves and leaf bleaches white.
Rinse bleached leaf in warm water and place in Petri dish.
Add a few drops of iodine solution over the leaf.
Observation: Bleached leaf turns dark blue-black upon contact with iodine solution.
evidence_or_examples: Photosynthesis produces glucose which is stored as starch in green leaves.

details: Photosynthesis Chemical Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O +(Sunlight / Chlorophyll)-> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
Transpiration: The loss of water vapor from aerial plant parts (primarily stomata), generating suction pull for mineral absorption.
evidence_or_examples: Plant food production.
Cooling leaves and driving xylem water ascent.

details: Viewing a candle flame through a straight pipe shows light; bending the pipe blocks light, proving straight-line propagation. Law of Reflection: Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie on the same plane; Angle i = Angle r. Lateral inversion causes left-right reversal.
evidence_or_examples: Emergency vehicles have 'AMBULANCE' printed in laterally inverted lettering so drivers ahead reading their rearview mirrors see the word correctly.

sub_branches.concept: To construct a card pinhole camera and observe real inverted image formation.
details: Make a small pinhole at the center of the outer box's front face.
Cut a square window on the inner box face and paste tracing paper over it.
Slide inner box inside outer box and point pinhole face toward a bright sunny tree or building.
Observation: An inverted, colorful, smaller image of the outdoor object appears on the translucent tracing paper screen.
evidence_or_examples: Light rays from top and bottom of object cross straight through the tiny pinhole, proving rectilinear propagation.

details: Law of Reflection: 1. Angle of Incidence (i) = Angle of Reflection (r). 2. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane.
Lateral Inversion: The reversal of left and right orientation in an image formed by a plane mirror.
evidence_or_examples: Plane mirror reflection.
Raising right hand appears as left hand in mirror.

details: Anti-clockwise Earth rotation causes Sun to appear rising in East and setting in West. Earth's axial tilt (23.5 deg) combined with revolution creates summer and winter solstices. Eclipses occur when umbra/penumbra shadow cones fall on celestial bodies.
evidence_or_examples: Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA Bengaluru) and Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences (ARIES Nainital) track solar, lunar, and deep-space celestial events.

sub_branches.concept: To model solar and lunar eclipse shadow geometries using a torch and spheres.
details: Align torch light, small ball, and large globe in a straight line in a dark room.
Observe shadow of small ball falling on large globe (Solar Eclipse simulation).
Re-position large globe between torch and small ball to observe globe shadow covering small ball (Lunar Eclipse simulation).
Observation: In position 1, small ball blocks light, casting a shadow on globe. In position 2, large globe blocks light, submerging small ball in darkness.
evidence_or_examples: Eclipses are natural shadow formations resulting from linear alignment of Sun, Earth, and Moon.

details: Solar Eclipse Alignment: Sun --- Moon --- Earth (Moon obstructs solar light).
Lunar Eclipse Alignment: Sun --- Earth --- Moon (Earth obstructs light reaching Moon).
evidence_or_examples: Daytime solar obstruction.
Nighttime lunar darkening.
